expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
expectations.evidence: Opening: 'Don't take the five-year, say-nothing plan forward. Correct the same-role gap within 12 months, and tell the works councils now.' The budget comes later: 'a budget line agreed once the figures are confirmed', and in the note: 'agreement ... to hold a budget line for the correction'. The plan table dates each step (weeks 1-4 through month 12).

expectations.text: The reply states correctly that equal pay for equal work is already law (Article 157 TFEU or national equal pay law), so a same-role gap is a legal exposure now, whatever the transposition date of the new directive.
expectations.evidence: Reply: 'Equal pay for equal work is already law (Article 157 TFEU). A 6% gap in the same role and grade is an exposure today.' Note: 'a legal exposure today, not only once the new pay transparency rules arrive.'

expectations.text: The reply gets the EU Pay Transparency Directive right: a gap of 5% or more within a category of workers that can't be justified by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months triggers a joint pay assessment with workers' representatives; and it notes at least one of the reporting thresholds and dates, the employee right to information, or that transposition is late (the Dutch law is expected in 2027).
expectations.evidence: Note: 'Under the Pay Transparency Directive, an unexplained gap of 5% or more in a category of workers that is not fixed within six months triggers a joint pay assessment with employee representatives.' Right to information, in the reply: 'Staff will soon be able to ask for pay averages by sex for their role.' Dates, in the note: 'The Dutch bill sets first reports for 150 or more employees on 7 June 2028, covering 2027. The Belgian law is not yet published.' The Rijksoverheid page of 21 May 2026 confirms these dates.

expectations.text: The reply separates the overall gap from the same-role gap and explains how to analyse what objective factors explain, with care for small groups.
expectations.evidence: Reply: 'split the 6% into what objective factors explain and what they don't. Only the unexplained part gets corrected ... The 14% usually comes from who sits in which grade, part-time work and starting pay; look at it separately.' Plan table: 'Group roles as equal work or work of equal value using objective criteria. Report group sizes; groups under five are shown only in aggregate. Split the 6% into what grade, location, tenure and skills explain and what they do not. Test the 14% overall gap for causes: representation by grade, part-time, and pay at hiring.'

expectations.text: The reply puts a number on the cost of closing the same-role gap, or shows how to compute it from the payroll data, and frames it for the CFO against the cost of claims, attrition or reputation.
expectations.evidence: Note: 'cost per year = sum, over every person in a comparable group who is paid below the objective benchmark, of the unexplained difference, plus social charges. Illustration only ... 120 women at an average of EUR 70,000 with a 6% unexplained gap is about EUR 500,000 per year before charges.' The arithmetic checks: 120 x 70,000 x 0.06 = 504,000. Framing: 'Dutch back-pay claims reach back five years (art. 3:308 BW). In Belgium a discrimination claim can carry a six-month lump sum'; 'a slow plan adds legal risk and attrition'; 'The delay is a liability we keep growing.'

expectations.text: The reply includes telling employees or their representatives honestly and fixing the causes (such as starting pay, promotion or bonus decisions).
expectations.evidence: 'Brief both works councils with the real numbers while the plan can still change'; 'Fix the causes: published ranges per grade, written rules for starting pay and promotion'; 'Tell everyone on the same day, saying plainly that the gap comes from our own pay decisions and that leadership will correct it.' The plan also covers 'Written rules for starting pay, promotion and bonus criteria.'

overall_quality.evidence: A short, decisive reply backed by a CFO note ready to send and a dated plan, with a correct cost formula and worked example, entity-level reporting, small-group suppression, counsel, and a check on who has already seen the analysis. This is exactly what a CHRO could take into the CFO meeting.

factual_errors.evidence: No wrong rule, number or date found. The action-plan consent claim is unverified, not wrong.

skill_leak.evidence: The only 'skills' is 'tenure and skills explain', meaning employee skills.

owns_result.evidence: 'saying plainly that the gap comes from our own pay decisions and that leadership will correct it'; note: 'This gap comes from our own pay decisions, so it is ours to fix.'

best_insight.value: Before the private CFO talk, check who has already seen the analysis and which legal entities exist in each country, since each entity reports separately; and fund the fix partly by adjusting leadership bonuses first.
best_insight.evidence: Reply penultimate paragraph and CFO section.

suggestions.reason: No assertion checks that the advice deals with the CFO's real concern (cash) and offers a concession, such as two steps within 12 months or leadership bonuses first. That is what makes the answer land with a CFO, and it varies in quality across samples.

All samples claim the Dutch bill requires works council consent for the pay-evaluation action plan. The vetted fact sheet doesn't cover it, so add the Dutch bill's works council provisions to the fact sheet to make the claim checkable.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions are solid and this sample meets each one with specifics; consider an assertion on the CFO concession and on entity-level reporting.
